title: PlayStation Portable
wiki_lead:
The PlayStation Portable (PSP) is a handheld game console developed and marketed by Sony Computer Entertainment. It was first released in Japan on December 12, 2004, in North America on March 24, 2005, and in PAL regions on September 1, 2005. It is the first handheld installment in the PlayStation line of consoles. As a seventh generation console, the PSP primarily competed with the Nintendo DS.
Development of the PSP was announced during E3 2003, and the console was unveiled at a Sony press conference on May 11, 2004. The system was the most powerful portable video game console at the time of its introduction, and was the first viable competitor to Nintendo's handheld consoles after many challengers such as Nokia's N-Gage and Sega's Game Gear had failed or underperformed. The PSP's advanced graphics capabilities made it a popular mobile entertainment device, which could connect to the PlayStation 3, select PlayStation 2 games, any computer with a USB interface, other PSP systems, and the Internet. The PSP also had a vast array of multimedia features such as video playback and audio playback, leading some to classify it as a portable media player. The PSP is the only handheld video game console to use an optical disc format, the Universal Media Disc, as its primary storage medium, and the format was used to distribute both games and media content.
The PSP was received positively by critics. The system sold over 80 million units during its ten-year lifetime, making it the best selling handheld video game console of all time not made by Nintendo. Several models of the console were released, including the PSP Street and the PSP Go. The system would go on to be succeeded by the PlayStation Vita, released in Japan in December 2011, which would have backward compatibility with PSP games that were released on the PlayStation Network through the PlayStation Store. Hardware shipments of the PSP ended worldwide in 2014.

The PlayStation Portable (PSP) is a handheld game console developed and marketed by Sony Computer Entertainment. It was first released in Japan on December 12, 2004, in North America on March 24, 2005, and in PAL regions on September 1, 2005. It is the first handheld installment in the PlayStation line of consoles. As a seventh generation console, the PSP primarily competed with the Nintendo DS.
Development of the PSP was announced during E3 2003, and the console was unveiled at a Sony press conference on May 11, 2004. The system was the most powerful portable video game console at the time of its introduction, and was the first viable competitor to Nintendo's handheld consoles after many challengers such as Nokia's N-Gage and Sega's Game Gear had failed or underperformed. The PSP's advanced graphics capabilities made it a popular mobile entertainment device, which could connect to the PlayStation 3, select PlayStation 2 games, any computer with a USB interface, other PSP systems, and the Internet. The PSP also had a vast array of multimedia features such as video playback and audio playback, leading some to classify it as a portable media player. The PSP is the only handheld video game console to use an optical disc format, the Universal Media Disc, as its primary storage medium, and the format was used to distribute both games and media content.
The PSP was received positively by critics. The system sold over 80 million units during its ten-year lifetime, making it the best selling handheld video game console of all time not made by Nintendo. Several models of the console were released, including the PSP Street and the PSP Go. The system would go on to be succeeded by the PlayStation Vita, released in Japan in December 2011, which would have backward compatibility with PSP games that were released on the PlayStation Network through the PlayStation Store. Hardware shipments of the PSP ended worldwide in 2014.


History


Pre-release
Prior to 2004, Sony was a leading company in the development and production of portable media players, producing product lines such as the Walkman for audio playback and the Watchman for live television. However, the handheld video game market would be largely dominated by Nintendo beginning with the Game Boy in 1989, with it and its successors outselling competition such as Sega's Game Gear and Bandai's WonderSwan line by significant margins. With the exception of the PocketStation in 1999, a PlayStation Memory Card capable of playing rudimentary games installed onto it, Sony would not make any attempts to enter into this market until into the sixth generation of video game consoles.
Sony Computer Entertainment first announced development of the PlayStation Portable at a press conference preceding E3 2003. Sony released extensive technical details and introduced the Universal Media Disc to be used for games, but did not show any hardware aside from that. Then-CEO Ken Kutaragi would dub the PSP the "Walkman of the 21st century", in reference to the console's multimedia capabilities. Initial reception was positive, with outlets such as IGN and Eurogamer impressed with the handheld's computing capabilities and looking forward to its potential as a gaming platform. An IDC analyst argued the PSP was the "first legitimate competitor to Nintendo's dominance in the handheld market".
The first concept images of the PSP appeared at a Sony corporate strategy meeting in November 2003, and featured a model with flat buttons and no analog stick. Some reviewers initially expressed concern about the lack of an analog stick, but by E3 2004, the final PSP design would be unveiled with a stick below the D-Pad. Sony released a list of 99 developer companies that pledged support for the new handheld, and demos for games such as Konami's Metal Gear Acid and Studio Liverpool's Wipeout Pure were shown at the conference.


Launch and early success
On October 18, 2004, Sony announced that the PSP base model would be launched in Japan on December 11 that year for ¥19,800 (about $181 USD in 2004) while the Value System would launch for ¥24,800 (about $226 USD). The launch was a success, with over 200,000 units sold on the first day of sales. On February 3, 2005, Sony announced that the PSP would be released in North America on March 24 in one configuration for an MSRP of $249 USD/$299 CAD. Some commentators expressed concern over the high price, which was almost $20 USD higher than that of the Japanese model and over $100 higher than the Nintendo DS. Despite these concerns, the PSP's North American launch was a success; Sony claimed 500,000 units were sold in the first two days of sales, though it was also reported that this figure was below expectations.
Launch PSP units in North America included the film Spider-Man 2 on a UMD disc. In April 2005, Sony would launch a dedicated line of movies for the system to retail, dubbed UMD Video for PSP, with the first titles for the format including Hellboy, Once Upon a Time in Mexico, Resident Evil: Apocalypse, and XXX.
The PSP was originally intended to have a simultaneous European and North American launch, but on March 15, 2005, Sony announced that the European and Oceania launch would be delayed due to high demand for the console in Japan and North America. In April, Sony announced that the PSP would be launched in Europe on September 1, 2005, for €249/£179. Sony defended the high price by saying North American consumers had to pay local sales taxes and that the Value Added Tax (sales tax) was higher in the UK than the US. Despite the high price, the PSP's launch in Europe was a success, with the console selling over 185,000 units in the UK. All stock of the PSP in the UK sold out within three hours of its launch, more than doubling the previous first-day sales record of 87,000 units set by the Nintendo DS. The system also enjoyed success in Oceania and the rest of Europe; over 25,000 units were pre-ordered in Australia, and nearly one million units were sold across Europe in the system's first week of sales.


Later years and discontinuation
Rumors of a successor to the PSP, often dubbed PSP2, would circulate the internet as early as 2009, with Eurogamer Spain reporting on reported technical specifications of the device. In January 2011, Sony would officially unveil the system at a "PlayStation Meeting" press conference, initially dubbing it NGP (Next Generation Portable). At E3 2011, the system would be officially dubbed PlayStation Vita, and would launch in Japan on December 17, 2011. At launch, the system supported digital PSP games via backwards compatibility.
Although Sony's game output would mostly cease after the Vita's launch, third party publishers would continue to support the system until 2016. Internationally, after the Vita launched, many PSP games released earlier in the system's life in Japan, such as The Legend of Heroes: Trails in the Sky SC and Brandish: The Dark Revenant, would be localized into English and released digitally, facilitating purchase and play on both PSP and Vita via backwards compatibility. 
By June 2014, Sony would cease shipments of PSP hardware worldwide. Sony reports that the system sold 80 million units in total. The PlayStation Store on PSP would be shut down in 2016, though compatible software purchased on a PS3, PS Vita, or web browser would still be downloadable; The web storefront was shut down in 2020, and the PS3 and PS Vita storefronts are set to shut down in 2027.


Hardware


PSP-1000

The launch model of the PlayStation Portable, referred to as the PSP-1000, features an oblong form factor measuring 6.7 by 2.9 by 0.9 inches (170 by 74 by 23 mm). The front of the system features the speakers as well as most of the system's controls, including the face buttons, d-pad, and analog stick, with other function buttons below the screen. It also contains the system's 4.3-inch (110 mm) TFT display, which is capable of 480 × 272 pixel display resolution and 24-bit color. The top of the system contains the two shoulder buttons, labelled L and R, the Wireless LAN and UMD eject switches, an IrDA infrared emitter, and a Mini USB port for data transfer. Below the system is the AC-in and 2-pin dock ports for charging, as well as the 3.5 mm audio and remote ports. The left and right sides of the system have the Memory Stick PRO Duo slot and power switch, respectively. The back gives access to the UMD drive and battery slot when either are uncovered. As a whole, the unit weighs 9.9 ounces (280 g).
Internally, the PSP uses two 333 MHz MIPS32 R4000 R4k-based CPUs, a GPU running at 166 MHz, and includes 32 MB main RAM, and 4 MB embedded DRAM split between the GPU and Media Engine. Although the CPU was natively 333 MHz, media would be locked to a maximum of 222 MHz until firmware 3.50 released in May 2007, at which point Sony allowed developers to release new games using higher clock speeds.
The PSP is powered by an 1800 mAh battery that provides about three to six hours of gameplay, four to five hours of video playback, and eight to eleven hours of audio playback. The battery completes a full charge after about 1.5 hours.


Revisions


PSP-2000

At E3 2007, Sony announced a new revision of the PSP. The PSP-2000, marketed in some regions as "PSP Slim & Lite", would first be released in Hong Kong on August 30, 2007, before releasing worldwide in September of that year. The revision would redesign the system to reduce weight and thickness, from 9.87 to 6.66 ounces (280 to 189 g) and from 0.91 to 0.73 inches (23 to 18.6 mm), respectively. In addition, the serial port was modified to add video out support, with support for 480i output of media via composite, S-Video, component, and D-Terminal, with the latter two also supporting game output in 480p. 
Other changes include improved WLAN modules, the removal of the IrDA emitter and 2-pin docking port, a simplified UMD drive mechanism, and a thinner, brighter LCD screen. To improve the poor loading times of UMD games on the original PSP, the internal memory (RAM and Flash ROM) was doubled from 32 MB to 64 MB, part of which now acting as a cache, also improving the web browser's performance.

To make the unit slimmer, the capacity of the PSP's battery was reduced from 1800 mAh to 1200 mAh starting with the PSP-2000. The original high-capacity batteries work on newer models with increased battery life, though the battery cover does not fit. In March 2008, Sony released the Extended Life Battery Kit in Japan, which included a bulkier 2200 mAh battery with fitting battery covers matching the many PSP variations available. All versions of the North American kit released in December 2008 were supplied with a black and a silver battery cover.


PSP-3000

The PSP-3000 was released in North America on October 14, 2008, in Japan on October 16, in Europe on October 17, and in Australia on October 23.
The PSP-3000, marketed in some areas as "PSP Slim & Lite" or "PSP Brite", was primarily sold as having an improved LCD screen with an increased color range, five times the contrast ratio, a halved pixel response time, new sub-pixel structure, and anti-reflective technology to reduce outdoor glare. The disc tray, logos, and buttons were all redesigned, and a microphone was added. Games could now be output in standard definition using the video-out cable, and more settings were added for the video out, such as flicker reduction, to allow users to tune the video output to their tastes. One outlet called this model "a minor upgrade".
On its release, the PSP-3000's screen was criticized for what appeared to be scan-lines and interlacing artifacts when objects were in motion. Due to the new screen using horizontal sub-pixels, and the blue sub-pixels appearing less luminant than their red and green counterparts, the blue sub-pixels would create faint horizontal lines across the screen. Sony stated the issue was inherent to the hardware and would not be fixed.

grok_lead: The PlayStation Portable (PSP) is a handheld video game console developed and marketed by Sony Computer Entertainment as the first portable entry in the PlayStation brand. It was initially released in Japan on December 12, 2004, followed by North America on March 24, 2005, and other regions shortly thereafter, featuring a 4.3-inch widescreen TFT LCD display with 480 Ã 272 resolution capable of rendering 16.77 million colors, a MIPS-based CPU clocked up to 333 MHz, and 32 MB of main memory. The device utilized proprietary Universal Media Discs (UMD) for game distribution and supported multimedia playback of video, audio, and photos, positioning it as an early portable media player alongside gaming capabilities that rivaled home consoles of the era. Over its production run from 2004 to 2014, multiple revised models including slimmer variants and the PSP Go, which lacked a UMD drive, were introduced, with cumulative worldwide sales exceeding 76 million units by the early 2010s, reflecting its commercial success despite challenges like short battery life and widespread software piracy.
